name: SES

profile.address: Kimbels Road, Palmyra Township, Pike County, Pennsylvania, 18464
profile.reading:
The SES Hawley Earth Station sits on Kimbels Road in Palmyra Township, Pike County, Pennsylvania, in the rural Pocono Mountains region of the state's northeastern corner, near the New York and New Jersey borders. Unlike a typical commercial colocation building, it is not a data center that leases server space to tenants. It is a satellite teleport, a ground facility built around large parabolic antennas that transmit and receive signals to and from geostationary satellites, supporting television distribution, government and military communications, maritime and aviation connectivity, and other satellite services rather than hosting racks of customer servers.

SES, the facility's operator, describes itself as a global space solutions company headquartered in Betzdorf, Luxembourg, operating a fleet of around 120 satellites alongside a global terrestrial network and more than 90 offices worldwide, serving sectors including aviation, energy, maritime, media, and government. SES grew into its current form through a series of acquisitions of national and regional satellite operators over the past three decades, consolidating what had been separately owned satellite fleets and ground infrastructure into one global network, of which a rural teleport site like Hawley is a small but functionally important piece.

Sites like this one are typically chosen for their radio quiet surroundings, favorable line of sight to the satellite arc, and distance from dense urban radio frequency interference, all of which describe Pike County's low density, forested terrain well. Because earth stations of this kind often carry government, defense, and broadcast traffic, operators routinely decline to publish the technical details that a commercial data center would advertise to attract customers, such as antenna count and size, uplink capacity, or backup power configuration, treating that information as sensitive rather than promotional. No square footage or power capacity figures for this site are published, and none are estimated here.

What can be documented is the facility's location, its function as part of SES's ground network, and the operator's scale and global business, while its specific technical footprint remains, by the nature of satellite ground infrastructure, outside the public record in a way that is itself typical for this category of facility rather than unusual.

reading:
SES S.A. is a publicly traded satellite operator headquartered in Betzdorf, Luxembourg, running a fleet of geostationary and medium earth orbit spacecraft together with a global ground network. It is carried in this registry because the single Pennsylvania building attached to it is tagged in OpenStreetMap as a data centre, and that tag is worth reading carefully. The site is a satellite earth station, not a colocation building. It leases no cabinets, hosts no customer servers and publishes no capacity sheet, and treating it as a data centre in the commercial sense will produce a wrong answer every time.

The early history of the site is unusually well documented for a building of its kind. The station on Kimbles Road in Palmyra Township, Pike County, was built by Comsat General, a subsidiary of the Communications Satellite Corporation, as one of seven original United States earth stations serving the COMSTAR satellites leased by AT&T. It was equipped with three 98 foot parabolic dishes and one 44 foot dish, plus a smaller dish with its own equipment shelter. AT&T Long Lines later took over tracking and control duties from Comsat General, and Hawley became the company's Satellite Operations Management Center, effectively mission control during satellite launches and the day to day operations centre for the fleet, connected terrestrially back toward Colesville, New Jersey through a chain of relay stations. Of the original seven stations, AT&T eventually took four forward for the Telstar 3 system. On 14 March 1997 Loral Space and Communications acquired AT&T Skynet Satellite Services, which became Loral Skynet, and Hawley continued the same functions under the new owner.

What is not established is the later half of the chain. Secondary and crowd sourced material places the site with RRsat and then inside SES media services, consistent with the consolidation that swept up regional teleport operators over the following two decades, but no primary document confirming that SES operates Hawley today has been located, and SES publishes no page for the site. The operator attribution on this row therefore rests on an OpenStreetMap tag rather than on a filing or a company statement, and it should be treated as provisional. The record that would settle it is the earth station licence file held in the Federal Communications Commission's international bureau system, which is where antenna diameters, transmit frequencies, coordinates and the licensee of record for a station like this actually live.

None of the four power figures this registry tracks exists for Hawley. There is no published IT load, no utility service size, no standby generator rating and no on site generation. An earth station's load profile is dominated by antenna drive motors, high power amplifiers on the uplink chain and the equipment shelters behind them, a shape quite unlike a raised floor hall. Sites of this type are chosen for radio quiet surroundings, an unobstructed view of the geostationary arc and distance from urban interference, which describes the low density forested terrain of the Pocono Mountains well. Because teleports frequently carry government, defence and broadcast traffic, operators routinely decline to publish the specifications a commercial colocation provider would advertise.
